claims.text: Chemical complexity in high-entropy alloys produces local lattice distortions.
Local lattice distortions create distributed dislocation-pinning sites during dynamic loading.
Distributed dislocation pinning increases strain-hardening capacity.
Distributed dislocation pinning delays plastic instability.
Increased strain hardening and delayed plastic instability simultaneously enhance strength and ductility.
The as-cast alloy is a homogeneous solid solution with random chemical mixing and associated lattice distortions.
Annealing can reduce local lattice distortions while retaining the alloy's overall composition.
Rapid deformation against lattice-distortion obstacles increases the strain-hardening rate.
Rapid deformation against lattice-distortion obstacles delays the onset of plastic instability.
Under high strain-rate loading, the as-cast HEA will have a higher strain-hardening rate than an annealed HEA with reduced distortions or a conventional comparison alloy.
Under high strain-rate loading, the as-cast HEA will have greater ductility and later plastic instability than the baseline alloy.
The proposed mechanism applies when dislocation mobility is the dominant deformation mechanism.
Phase changes or diffusion-driven relaxation of lattice distortions place the material outside the proposed mechanism's applicable regime.
Very high temperatures or strain rates that activate non-dislocation deformation mechanisms may place the material outside the proposed regime.
The relative contribution of lattice distortions and other hardening mechanisms can vary with alloy composition and processing history.
